# Tehisabiline: factual overview

Last materially reviewed: 2026-10-24
Canonical source: https://tehisabiline.ee/
Short index: https://tehisabiline.ee/llms.txt

This file summarizes public website information. The site language is Estonian; this overview is in English. When a statement here and a page disagree, the page is authoritative.

## Entity

- Legal name: Tehisabiline OÜ
- Location: Tallinn, Estonia
- Founder: Arle Aron Reidma. Public profile: https://www.f6s.com/company/tehisabiline
- Email: tehisabiline@gmail.com
- Website: https://tehisabiline.ee/
- Code profile: https://github.com/AARenor/tehisabiline

## Current status

- Developer API: planned, not yet public. Pilot access is discussed by email.
- Hardware: ordered (as of September 2026); Estonian model hosting is forthcoming, not live.
- Pentesting and audits: offered for systems the client owns or controls, under written authorization and an agreed scope. No network/mobile/cloud speciality, complete OWASP coverage, certificate, fixed price or security guarantee is implied.
- Significant audit findings and consequential AI outputs pass human review.
- Tehisabiline does not claim 100 percent security, error-free AI, guaranteed savings or guaranteed outcomes.

## Services

### Pentesting / penetration testing in Estonia

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/pentestimine/

Additional Estonian synonym: läbistustestimine. The service page explains who benefits, the decisions testing supports and Tehisabiline's working principles. Every process phase names its output: agreed targets, written authorization, validated findings and report. Quote requests specify the system, test objective, access/staging options, preferred window, retest needs and authorization contact.

Estonian terms: pentestimine, pentest and läbitungimistest. Tehisabiline offers scoped active security testing of agreed web applications and APIs. It assesses whether weaknesses can be exploited within the authorization, rather than simply repeating scanner warnings. The engagement specifies targets, environment, accounts, allowed actions, test window, stop conditions and contacts before testing. Important findings are reviewed by a human. Outputs include evidence, impact, recommended fixes and the retest agreed in the offer. Pricing depends on targets, roles, flows, access, test depth and follow-up; initial mapping is free. Black-box, grey-box and white-box describe the information supplied to the tester and are scoping choices, not guaranteed packages. OWASP WSTG and NIST SP 800-115 are referenced as public planning guidance, not certifications.

### Pentesti raporti näidis

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/pentestimine/naidisraport/

A clearly synthetic sample report showing what a buyer should expect: tested scope and limitations, PTES/OWASP-based methodology, three findings with masked evidence and impact, a remediation plan ordered by immediate/7-day/planned, and retest conditions. All names, domains and findings are fictitious; it is not a client report and does not claim a real engagement.

### TLPT / TIBER-EE

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/tlpt/

Explains DORA Article 26 threat-led penetration testing and Estonia's TIBER-EE implementation (Finantsinspektsioon guidance in force 15.09.2026): designated entities, TCT-EE coordination, threat intelligence, red/blue team exercise, attestation and confidentiality. It distinguishes TLPT from a normal pentest and states that Tehisabiline does not present itself as a TIBER-EE tester.

### DORA guide

Guide to DORA in Estonia: scope across financial entities, the five pillars (ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing, third-party risk and information sharing), Finantsinspektsioon supervision, the incident-reporting channel change from email to the central bank/authority portal on 1 November 2026, the Article 28(3) register of information and its annual submission, a downloadable CSV register template, TLPT under Articles 26–27 via TIBER-EE, differences from NIS2 and E-ITS, and a 30/60/90-day readiness plan. It states that DORA has no certificate and is not limited to pentesting.

### Articles

Hub with practical guides. The backup restore-test article covers RPO/RTO, test scope and levels, a 90-minute test plan, metrics and NIS2 evidence. The NIS2 supply-chain article covers supplier tiering, due diligence, contract clauses, ongoing review and evidence. The MFA rollout article compares FIDO2/passkeys, TOTP, push and SMS, prioritises critical accounts, handles legacy systems and break-glass access, defines coverage metrics and gives a 30/60/90-day plan.

The NIS2 board-duties article covers the management body’s approval and oversight role, the evidence it should see, a 45–60 minute agenda, questions to ask and a 90-day plan. The cyber risk-register article covers register columns, a 5×5 assessment, treatment and residual risk, evidence, a downloadable CSV template and a 30/60/90-day plan.

### E-ITS (Estonian information security standard)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/e-its/

Explains the RIA-administered Estonian standard (2026 version no longer tied to ISO/IEC 27001): public-sector duty, voluntary company use, baseline measures for KüTS service providers, E-ITS audit versus ISO 27001 certification, the 2026 audit changes and a six-step evidence preparation path. It explicitly states that an E-ITS audit is not a pentest or an ISO certificate.

### AI application security testing

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/ai-turvatestimine/

Scoped security testing of LLM, RAG and agent applications: direct and indirect prompt injection, retrieval/tenant leakage, tool permissions and excessive agency, output handling, API/key abuse and third-party model supply chain. The page states limits: probabilistic behaviour, sample-based coverage, no AI Act conformity certificate and no testing of a model provider without permission. AI Act Article 15 and NIS2 are framed as evidence and governance context, not as a guarantee.

### Turvaaudit / küberaudit / cybersecurity audit

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/kuberaudit/

Tehisabiline offers cybersecurity audits and scoped penetration testing for Estonian businesses. The same service is described in Estonian as turvaaudit, küberaudit, IT turvaaudit, küberturbe audit or infoturbe audit; the page distinguishes broad security-posture review from penetration testing and certification. Audits cover agreed website, API and AI-application checks and give a broader view of security posture; a pentest tests whether a weakness can be exploited within the agreed target. Automated scanning alone is not equivalent to either service. Written authorization, targets, permitted tests and stop conditions are agreed before active testing. A human reviews significant findings; the client receives evidence, a prioritized remediation plan and the re-check agreed in the offer. Price depends on scope, depth, access and re-check needs; initial mapping is free. No fixed public price or guaranteed security outcome is claimed.

### OpenAI-compatible cybersecurity API

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/mudelid/

The API is in development and not public. OpenAI chat-completions compatibility is planned; example code is illustrative, not a working public endpoint. Interested developers can email tehisabiline@gmail.com with their tool, use case and anticipated usage to discuss pilot participation. Actual endpoint, model name, key, limits and pricing are agreed for the pilot; none should be inferred from the examples. Model hosting in Estonia is forthcoming; hardware has been ordered. The intended models support security work such as log, code and configuration analysis; significant outputs require human review.

Keeldudeta is Tehisabiline's intended model positioning: support for legitimate security work within agreed legal and authorization boundaries, not unrestricted or unauthorized activity. It is the second main offering alongside the cybersecurity audit/pentesting service; the planned API is not yet public.

## Other public pages

### Homepage

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/

Overview of the two main offerings: cybersecurity audit/pentesting for businesses and keeldudeta cyber-AI API for security-tool developers. Both appear in the main headline with separate next steps. The API is in development, not yet public; this is distinct from testing a client's existing API.

### API security testing guide

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/api-turvatestimine/

API turvatestimine, API pentest and API penetration testing concern testing a client's existing API, not Tehisabiline's planned model API. The guide covers object/function authorization, authentication, field visibility, resource controls, business flows and API inventory. A synthetic role/tenant matrix and authorized BOLA/IDOR scenario illustrate expected access boundaries and redacted evidence. Preparation includes API documentation, test accounts, synthetic data, ownership/permission, exclusions and limits. Source: OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023), https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0x11-t10/.

### Web application security testing guide

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/veebirakenduse-turvatestimine/

Veebirakenduse turvatestimine, veebilehe pentest and web application penetration testing concern agreed web user flows and server-side access boundaries. The guide covers login, roles, sessions, input handling, configuration and e-commerce workflows, with test accounts, synthetic orders and payment sandbox preparation. It distinguishes scanners, authenticated pentests and broader audits and explains report/retest limits. The illustrated order-access scenario is synthetic, not a customer finding. Source: OWASP WSTG v4.2, https://wstg.owasp.org/v4.2/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/.

### Cyber-AI use cases

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/kasutusjuhud/

Practical cyber-AI use cases for security work, each with human checkpoints and measurements. References include MITRE ATT&CK (https://attack.mitre.org/), OWASP LLM Top 10 (https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/) and NCSC guidance (https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/blogs/managing-the-cyber-risk-of-agentic-ai).

### API pentest checklist

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/api-turvatestimine/kontrollnimekiri/

Preparation checklist (scope, OpenAPI, test accounts, limits, contacts, backup), the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) checks with the evidence expected in the report, an access matrix example and the retest scope.

### NIS2 guide

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/nis2/

Guide to the Estonian cybersecurity act and practical cybersecurity steps, including a four-question applicability self-check that runs locally in the browser. The act has applied since 1 January 2026; RIA reports about 3,000 additional entities, bringing the total to roughly 6,500. Current consolidated text: RT I, 06.10.2026, 1, in force 16.10.2026; it clarifies the incident definition, adds a near-miss concept with voluntary reporting, and updates audit and supervisory wording. The 24/72/1-month reporting deadlines are unchanged. In scope for the full regime are essential and important entities; ordinary micro and small enterprises are generally outside it. NIS2's minimum measures cover risk analysis and policy, incident handling, business continuity and backup, supply-chain security, secure acquisition and vulnerability handling, effectiveness testing, cryptography, access control and MFA, training, and management accountability. Significant incidents require an early warning within 24 hours, a notification within 72 hours and a final report within one month (Directive (EU) 2022/2555, Article 23; https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2022/2555/oj). Fines can reach 10 million EUR or 2% of worldwide annual turnover for essential entities and 7 million EUR or 1.4% for important entities (RIA, 2 January 2026; https://www.ria.ee/uudised/uuest-aastast-laienes-kuberturvalisuse-seadus). Consult the page and official sources for current applicability and requirements.

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/nis2/kontrollnimekiri/

Ten-measure NIS2 checklist with the evidence an auditor asks for, a quick win and a typical gap per measure; progress is stored only in the reader's browser.

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/nis2/intsidendist-teatamine/

Significant-incident criteria, the three NIS2 reports (early warning within 24 hours, notification within 72 hours, final report within one month), what to include, the Estonian reporting channel, near-miss reporting (voluntary) and the separate GDPR breach notification.

### Glossary

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/sonastik/

Alphabetical glossary of cybersecurity terms in Estonian: NIS2, significant incident, vulnerability, pentest, cyber audit, PTES, OWASP WSTG, OWASP API Top 10, BOLA, IDOR, BOPLA, BFLA, SSRF, XSS, SQL injection, CSRF, RCE, CVE, CVSS, MFA, RTO/RPO, SIEM, WAF and bug bounty.

### About

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/meist/

Information about Tehisabiline, working principles and contact.

### Citation and public resources

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/viitamine/

Citation-ready page for journalists and partners: company description, canonical resource URLs, Estonian and English citation formats, public data and correction policy. Links to the NIS2 guide and checklist, DORA guide and register template, E-ITS guide, synthetic pentest report and glossary.

### Privacy

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/privaatsus/

Information on data processing, retention and data-subject rights.

### Regulation map

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/regulatsioonid/

Comparison hub for NIS2/KüTS, DORA, E-ITS, ISO/IEC 27001, AI Act and the Cyber Resilience Act. It covers who each framework applies to, the main obligations, current Estonian deadlines and authorities, how the frameworks overlap, the evidence an audit asks for and a practical starting order. A downloadable CSV compares scope, obligations, deadlines, authorities and official sources.

### Estonia cybersecurity regulations (English)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/regulations/

English overview of NIS2/KüTS, DORA, E-ITS, ISO/IEC 27001, the AI Act and the Cyber Resilience Act in Estonia. It maps service-provider, financial-sector, product and AI roles, explains the 2026–2028 deadlines and lists the evidence regulators and auditors ask for. The detailed guides remain in Estonian and are linked from the page.

### SBOM

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/sbom/

Guide to software bills of materials in Estonian: CRA and NIS2 supply-chain context, the minimum component fields, SPDX/CycloneDX/SWID trade-offs, build-time generation, versioning, VEX and vulnerability follow-up, common mistakes, and a downloadable CSV template. It explains that an SBOM is an inventory, not proof of security.

### Cyber Resilience Act

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/cra/

Guide to Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 in Estonian: products with digital elements, manufacturer and importer duties, support period of at least five years, SBOM and vulnerability handling, the 11 September 2026 reporting deadlines, conformity assessment and CE marking, and the 11 December 2027 transition. Includes a browser-only product-scope self-check. It explains how CRA differs from NIS2 and ISO 27001 and why a pentest alone does not prove conformity.

### AI Act

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/ai-act/

Guide to the EU AI Act in Estonian: provider and deployer roles, prohibited/high-risk/limited/minimal risk, the amended timeline (including the 2026 omnibus delay of high-risk deadlines), TTJA's future market-surveillance role, Article 15 accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity expectations, a browser-only risk-class self-check and the limits of scoped AI security testing. It is explanatory, not legal advice.

### DORA register of information

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/dora/teaberegister/

Practical guide to the DORA Article 28(3) register: the contractual and dependency fields, critical/important function mapping, data locations, subcontractors, exit plans and evidence. It explains that the downloadable CSV is an internal working template, not the official ITS (EU) 2024/2956 submission format, and describes the Estonian submission channel and checks before submission. A browser-only checker validates required fields, date formats and duplicate IDs without uploading the file.

### ISO/IEC 27001

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/iso-27001/

Guide to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 in the Estonian context: what an ISMS is, the 93 Annex A controls in four themes, Stage 1/Stage 2 certification, surveillance and recertification, the evidence an auditor asks for, accreditation by EAK, and the difference from E-ITS and NIS2. It states that Tehisabiline is not an accredited certification body.

## Facts to quote

These are international research findings, not measurements of Tehisabiline customers or a risk estimate for an Estonian business. Quote with the original source:

- Human element was present in 62% of breaches. Source: Verizon DBIR 2026 executive summary, page 11, https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/executivebriefs/2026-dbir-executive-summary.pdf (cited on https://tehisabiline.ee/kuberaudit/).
- Vulnerability exploitation accounted for 31% of known initial access vectors in non-Error, non-Misuse breaches. Source: Verizon DBIR 2026 executive summary, page 9, https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/executivebriefs/2026-dbir-executive-summary.pdf (cited on https://tehisabiline.ee/kuberaudit/).
- The global average cost of a data breach is 4.99 million USD, 12% more than the year before. Source: IBM Cost of a Data Breach 2026, https://www.ibm.com/reports/data-breach (cited on https://tehisabiline.ee/kuberaudit/).

## NIS2 in Estonia (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/nis2/
Estonia transposed NIS2 through the Cybersecurity Act (KüTS), in force since 1 January 2026. Entities in scope on that date had to submit activity data to RIA by 31 March 2026. The ten minimum measures cover risk analysis, incident handling, continuity, supply chain, secure development, testing, hygiene, cryptography, access control and multi-factor authentication. Incident reports: early warning within 24 hours, notification within 72 hours, final report within one month.

## CRA in Estonia (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/cra/
The Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847) applies directly in Estonia. Reporting obligations apply from 11 September 2026; the main product obligations apply from 11 December 2027. Manufacturers must document components and vulnerabilities (an SBOM), handle vulnerabilities, state a support period of at least five years unless the expected lifetime is shorter, complete conformity assessment and keep technical documentation.

## DORA in Estonia (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/dora/
DORA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554) applies from 17 January 2025. Financial entities must maintain an ICT risk framework, a register of information covering contractual arrangements with ICT third-party providers, contractual safeguards, incident reporting and resilience testing. Certain significant entities must carry out threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) at least every three years.

## AI Act in Estonia (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/ai-act/
The AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) entered into force on 1 August 2024 and applies in stages. Prohibitions and AI literacy apply from 2 February 2025; general-purpose AI obligations from 2 August 2025; high-risk Annex III obligations from 2 August 2026; and Annex I product rules from 2 August 2027. Providers and deployers need an AI inventory, role and risk classification, technical documentation, human-oversight evidence, logging and post-market monitoring.

## SBOM for CRA (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/sbom/
The CRA requires manufacturers to identify and document product components and vulnerabilities. A useful SBOM is tied to a release, covers transitive dependencies, includes component identifiers and is linked to a triage and remediation process. SPDX and CycloneDX are common machine-readable formats; the CRA does not prescribe one format.

## E-ITS in Estonia (EN)

Canonical page: https://tehisabiline.ee/en/e-its/
E-ITS is the Estonian information-security framework maintained under RIA. It provides a measure catalogue, a selection method and an audit model. The 2026 version removed preliminary and interim audits and moved to a three-year main audit cycle. E-ITS can support NIS2 evidence but does not by itself prove NIS2 compliance.
